x: Glossary Plain-English guide Government money comes with a lot of jargon. Here is every term on this site, explained simply first, with more detail after. Anywhere on the site, a word with a dotted underline can be tapped for its short explanation. Community Redevelopment Agencies Property taxes and your bill Budgets and where money comes from How we label spending on this site Contracts, land and borrowing Public records Community Redevelopment Agencies Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) A savings jar for one neighborhood that needs fixing up. When the neighborhood's property gets more valuable, the extra tax money goes into the jar, and it can only be spent in that neighborhood. Florida law lets a city or county create a CRA for an area it officially finds run-down. The city commission usually acts as the CRA's board. It follows a written redevelopment plan and has an end date. Example: Lynn Haven's CRA covers about 695 acres around Ohio and Florida Avenues. CRA district The line drawn on the map around the neighborhood a CRA covers. Money raised inside the line is spent inside the line. Some CRAs have several districts. Panama City has four: Downtown, Downtown North, St. Andrews and Millville. Tax increment (TIF) The extra property tax a neighborhood brings in because its property became worth more after the CRA started. That extra is what fills the CRA's jar. On the day a CRA starts, the total property value inside it is written down. Every year after, the city and the county each pay into the CRA's trust fund the taxes on any value above that starting number. TIF stands for tax increment financing. Example: If a district was worth $100 million when it started and is worth $150 million now, the taxes on the $50 million difference go to the CRA. Base year The starting snapshot of how much all the property in a CRA was worth. Only growth above this number pays into the CRA. The base year is set when the CRA is created and stays the same for the life of the CRA. CRA trust fund The CRA's own bank account. Tax increment goes in, and by law it can only be spent on that CRA's plan. State law (Chapter 163, Part III) requires each CRA to keep its money in a separate trust fund and report how it was spent every year. Sunset date The day a CRA is scheduled to end. After that, the extra tax money goes back to the city and county budgets. A city can vote to extend a CRA's life. Lynn Haven extended its CRA to 2043 in January 2026. TIF rebate A deal where the CRA gives a builder back part of the new taxes their project creates, for a set number of years, to help get the project built. The rebate is paid only after the owner pays the full tax bill, and it has a maximum amount. Example: Panama City approved five TIF rebate awards downtown in December 2024. Façade or storefront grant Money a CRA gives a business owner to fix up the front of their building, usually matching what the owner spends. Most programs are 50/50: the CRA pays half, up to a limit, after the work is done. Property taxes and your bill Property tax (ad valorem tax) A tax based on what your house or land is worth. More valuable property pays more. Ad valorem is Latin for 'according to value.' Several governments each charge their own property tax, and all of them show up on one bill from the Tax Collector. Taxing authority Any government allowed to put a property tax on your bill, like the county, the school board or your city. Each one sets its own rate every year at a public hearing. Millage (mills) How property tax rates are written. One mill means $1 of tax for every $1,000 your property is taxed on. A rate of 5.5 mills is the same as 0.55%. Your bill adds up the mills from every taxing authority that covers your address. Example: 5 mills on a home taxed at $200,000 is $1,000 a year. Just value The Property Appraiser's estimate of what your property would sell for. It is set as of January 1 each year. Assessed value Your property's value after any limits on how fast it can go up. For a homestead, it usually rises more slowly than the market. Florida's Save Our Homes rule keeps a homestead's assessed value from rising more than 3% a year, or the rate of inflation if lower. Taxable value The number your tax is actually figured on: the assessed value minus any exemptions. It can be different for school taxes and other taxes, because one homestead exemption does not apply to school taxes. Homestead exemption A discount on property taxes for the home you live in full time, as long as you apply for it. The first $25,000 of value is exempt from all property taxes. A second amount, on assessed value above $50,000, is exempt from every tax except school taxes. It was $25,000 until 2024 and now rises with inflation: $25,722 in 2025 and $26,411 in 2026. Example: In 2025, a homestead assessed at $200,000 was taxed on $149,278 by the city and county and on $175,000 by the school board. Rolled-back rate The tax rate that would bring in the same money as last year from the same properties. If a government picks a higher rate, the law calls it a tax increase, even if the rate didn't change. New construction is left out of the calculation, so growth alone does not count as an increase. TRIM notice The postcard you get each August showing your proposed taxes and when the public hearings are. TRIM stands for Truth in Millage, Florida's law that sets the steps governments must follow before raising property taxes. Non-ad valorem assessment A flat fee on your tax bill for a service, like garbage pickup or fire protection. It isn't based on what your property is worth. It appears on the same bill as property taxes but is calculated per home, per acre or per unit instead of by value. MSTU An extra county tax area that pays for services in only part of the county, usually the areas outside cities. MSTU stands for Municipal Service Taxing Unit. Required Local Effort The school tax rate the state tells every school district to charge so it can get its share of state school money. The Legislature sets it each year. School boards can add a small discretionary rate and a capital rate for buildings. Save Our Homes cap A limit on how fast a homestead's taxed value can go up: 3% a year, or less if inflation is lower. Rentals, businesses and second homes have a looser 10% limit. The limits apply to assessed value, not to tax rates. Amendment 3 would lower the 10% limit to 5% for non-school taxes. Levy The total property tax a government collects in a year: its rate times all the taxable value in its area. Budgets and where money comes from Revenue Estimating Conference The state's team of economists that estimates how much money a new law or amendment would add or take away. Staff from the Legislature, the Governor's office and the Office of Economic and Demographic Research agree on one official estimate. Example: For Amendment 3, it estimated the loss for every county, city and special district. Fiscal year (FY) A government's budget year. In Florida it runs from October 1 to September 30. It is named for the year it ends in. Example: FY2026 runs from October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026. General fund A government's main checking account for everyday services like police, parks and running city hall. Most property tax goes here. Money for special purposes is kept in separate funds. Enterprise fund An account for a service you pay for directly, like water and sewer. The bills you pay cover the service. These run like a small business inside the government. Special revenue fund Money that by law can only be spent on one thing, like gas tax for roads or a CRA's trust fund. State shared revenue Money the state collects, mostly from sales tax, and sends back to cities and counties. The biggest piece is the half-cent sales tax program. Cities and counties also get revenue-sharing money based on population and other factors. Charges for services Money a government earns by charging for things it provides, like water bills, garbage pickup, permits and park fees. Intergovernmental revenue Money one government gets from another, like federal grants or state shared revenue. Constitutional officers The elected county officials named in Florida's constitution: the sheriff, property appraiser, tax collector, clerk of court and supervisor of elections. Each has its own budget, and the county pays for most of them. Audit / annual financial report A yearly check of a government's books by outside accountants, to make sure the numbers add up and the rules were followed. Florida governments must file their audits and financial reports with the state. This site uses those filings. How we label spending on this site Spent The record says the money was actually paid out. Committed A contract or award has been approved, but not all of the money has been paid yet. Budgeted Money set aside in a plan. It may or may not be spent. Proposed An idea or request that hasn't been approved. Left out of totals Shown on the site, but not added into the totals, so the same dollar is never counted twice. Examples: a change order that is already part of a project total, a possible duplicate, or money that isn't from the CRA. Contracts, land and borrowing Change order An approved change to a contract after it is signed, which often adds cost or time. Right-of-way The land a road sits on plus the strip alongside it for sidewalks, utilities and drainage. Widening a road often means buying more right-of-way. Eminent domain When a government buys private land for a public project even if the owner doesn't want to sell. A court decides the fair price. The court process is called condemnation. Bond A way for a government to borrow money now and pay it back with interest over many years, like a mortgage. The yearly payments are called debt service. Community Development District (CDD) A special government created for one development to build and pay for its roads, pipes and other basics. The property owners there pay for it. Interlocal agreement A contract between two governments, like a city and the county. Public records Public records request Asking a government to show you or send you its records. In Florida, anyone can ask, and you don't have to say why. Florida's public records law is Chapter 119 of the Florida Statutes. Governments can charge for copies and for large amounts of staff time. Check register A government's list of every payment it made: who got paid, how much, when and for what. It is the most direct way to see where money went, and most cities don't post it online.

x: What's new Updates New pages, new data and corrections, newest first. Subscribe with any feed reader to get them as they happen: RSS feed . BayCounty.me launched on Oct 20, 2026. The first entries below are the initial pages going live. From here on, each new dataset, data refresh and correction gets its own dated entry. Change log Oct 22, 2026 A privacy page, and data for the iPhone app. A new privacy page says what the site and the BayCounty.me iPhone app collect: no accounts, no ads and no tracking. The site now also publishes the files the app reads, in /data/app: the tax and Amendment 3 calculators, the glossary, company and people profiles and the money map. They hold the same information the pages already show. /privacy · API Oct 21, 2026 Company pages, and one map of public money. Every company with more than one record now has its own page: its contracts, change orders, payments, CRA money, gifts from the business to campaigns, and the votes that approved its contracts with how each member voted. A gift near a vote does not show why anyone voted the way they did. A new map shows CRA spending and 1,062 sales tax projects over CRA districts and city limits. Hurricane Michael projects are not on it because FEMA does not publish their locations. /public-money/vendors · /public-money/map · Contracts · Who Gets Paid · Money Map Oct 21, 2026 New votes, FY2027 budgets, contracts and tourism payments. Added 30 votes (Panama City CRA and Commission, Callaway Commission and CRA) with each member's vote; the FY2027 budgets adopted in September for all nine governments; 17 contracts, mostly Springfield and Callaway; and tourism agency payments for 18 more months, each checked against the register's printed totals. Bay County Commission minutes after June 16 are not posted yet. How They Voted · Tax Dollars · Contracts · Who Gets Paid · CRA Spending Oct 21, 2026 My Address: your officials, nearby spending, and privacy. My Address now links each local official to how they voted and to campaign money, lists CRA spending and sales tax projects near you, and links to your government's contracts, meetings and budget. To protect owners' privacy it no longer shows which kinds of exemptions a parcel gets (such as disability or veteran exemptions); it shows homestead and one total for all other exemptions. My Address · Exemptions Oct 21, 2026 Share any view; alerts you choose; Spanish pages. Filters now stay in the page link, so you can share exactly what you are looking at. Search results open the record itself. You can now get an email when a contract over an amount you pick is approved, when a board member votes, or when an agenda mentions a word you choose, and change what you follow at any time. Tax Dollars, Fees and Bills, Exemptions, Elections and Meetings are now in Spanish. Email Alerts · Search · What's new Oct 21, 2026 Contracts: how much each contract grew. Change orders are now added up for each contract and measured against its original amount, instead of listed one by one. Of the 22 contracts whose original amount is known, 12 grew by more than 10%, the point where Bay County and Panama City rules require board approval for the added cost. Each bar opens to its change orders, reasons and sources. Contracts whose original amount wasn't in the agendas are listed separately, and where an agenda states the new contract total, that total is used. Every individual change order is still listed below. Contracts Oct 21, 2026 Contracts: one name per company, and company cards. Agendas, check registers and campaign reports spell the same company many ways, so the contract winners list was splitting some firms into two or more entries. The 322 contracts used 206 spellings; they now resolve to the companies behind them. Marshall Brothers, for example, had been listed at $11.1M and is now ranked sixth at $24.0M. A new Look up a company section shows everything on the site for one company: contracts by government next to what each government paid it (where a check register shows it), change orders, emergency purchases, campaign gifts from the company, and votes on its contracts by officials it gave to. Insurance pools owned by governments (Florida League of Cities, PGIT) are no longer counted as contractor wins. Contracts Oct 21, 2026 Money map: full roll calls on donor contract votes. The table of votes on a donor's contract now shows each vote once, with every board member's vote, not only the members who received a gift from the business. Members who got a gift are listed first, with the amount and date. Most of these contracts passed unanimously on the consent agenda. One vote that had been left out was added: Panama City's June 24, 2025 award of the Millville plant generator bid to Marshall Brothers, which the minutes record under an unrelated plat item. Money Map Oct 21, 2026 Sort, filter and download every list. Every table and list on the site can now be sorted by clicking a column heading, filtered with a search box (and drop-downs where a column has a few values), and downloaded as a CSV of exactly the rows on screen, in the order shown. Lists open newest first, then A to Z; upcoming meetings open soonest first. What's new Oct 21, 2026 An API for BayCounty.me. Every dataset on the site is now available through a free, read-only API with filtering, sorting and CSV output, plus an MCP server so AI assistants can look up and cite these records directly. API Oct 21, 2026 Correction: Money map. The first version of the Money map overstated connections. It counted a donor's contracts again for every official the donor gave to, which roughly doubled the government totals, and it drew lines from officials to governments they don't serve on. The map now puts each donor in the middle: campaign gifts on one side, the governments that pay the donor on the other, each counted once. It marks only gifts to an official whose own government pays that donor, and lists the recorded votes those officials cast on that donor's contracts. The heat map that credited contract dollars to individual officials was removed. Money Map Oct 21, 2026 Who's running in 2026. Every local race on Bay County ballots this year, with each candidate's platform in their own words, links to their campaigns, and their campaign money: what they raised and spent, how much came from individuals, organizations and their own pockets, and every business or committee that gave. Exemptions · My Address Oct 21, 2026 School Board votes, and more city votes. How They Voted now includes 104 School Board votes from January 2024 to September 2026 with each member's vote, including budgets, millage and major contracts; all 2024 Panama City Beach council votes, including the FY2025 budget; and Springfield votes from mid-2024 to October 2026, including both final budget hearings. Payments by Visit Panama City Beach, Destination Panama City and the Mexico Beach CDC, read from the Clerk of Court's check registers and checked against each month's printed total. Who Gets Paid Oct 21, 2026 Every bond, note and loan. Debt Oct 21, 2026 A page for each government. Bay County, the School Board and each of the seven cities now have one page that pulls together who runs it, its budget and property tax rate, debt, audit findings, recorded votes, contracts, projects and upcoming meetings. Governments Oct 21, 2026 Compare governments side by side. Pick any governments and compare budgets, tax rates, debt and staffing, in total or per resident. Compare Oct 21, 2026 Upcoming public meetings. Every board's next meetings, with agenda links and the money items on each agenda, checked daily. Records Request Oct 21, 2026 Open data downloads. Every dataset on the site, as CSV and JSON files you can open in a spreadsheet, with a description of each column. Open Data Oct 21, 2026 Zoning and development near your address. My Address now shows the zoning and future land use at the address, development projects and orders within half a mile, recent rezonings, and conditional uses nearby. My Address Oct 21, 2026 BayCounty.me en español. My Address, the records request tool and the glossary are now available in Spanish. Mi dirección, solicitudes de registros y el glosario, en español. My Address now finds addresses typed with full street types (Drive, Avenue, Boulevard), directions (North, West), highway forms (Hwy 98, US 98, County Road 2321), Saint or St., spelled-out numbers (Tenth Street), MLK, unit numbers, and a city, state and ZIP on the end. Updates
What BayCounty.me is, where its information comes from, and how to send a correction.
x: About About BayCounty.me BayCounty.me is an independent project that collects Bay County, Florida public records and turns them into maps and tables anyone can read. It starts with how local governments spend public money and will grow from there. Where the information comes from Everything on the site comes from documents the public can already request or download: city and county budgets, annual reports, audits filed with the Florida Auditor General, council and commission resolutions, Bay County GIS map layers, and reporting by local newsrooms. Each figure carries a link to its source. What the labels mean Spent : the record reports the money as paid. Committed : a contract or award has been approved but is not fully paid. Budgeted or Proposed : a plan or appropriation, not a payment. Totals count each dollar once. When one record is part of another (a change order inside a project total, for example), it stays visible but is left out of the totals. Corrections, records and questions Found an error, or have a public record that fills a gap? Send it here. Corrections are dated on the page they affect and listed under What's new . What's this about? A correction A record or tip A question Something else Page (optional) Not about a specific page Home My Address Search About What's new Bay County Bay District Schools All governments Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Parker Mexico Beach Compare governments Who runs Bay County Tax Dollars Fees & Bills Tourist Tax Exemptions Amendment 3 Budget Explorer CRA Spending Sales Tax Projects Public Money Map Hurricane Michael Contracts How They Voted Campaign Money Money Map Who Gets Paid Vendors Debt Audit Findings 2026 Elections Meetings Email alerts Request a record Send a correction Glossary Open data API What's new Message Name (optional) Email (only if you want a reply) Website Send message Messages go to the BayCounty.me team at Flux Labs. Your email address is used only to reply and is never published. To send a document, include a link, or email hello@fluxlabs.net . Who runs it BayCounty.me is built and hosted by Flux Labs , a managed IT services company in Panama City.

s: About
What BayCounty.me and its iPhone app collect: no accounts, no ads, no tracking.
x: Privacy BayCounty.me doesn't sell, share or track you. There are no accounts, no ads and no tracking cookies, on the website or in the iPhone app. The website Visits. The site counts page views with Vercel Web Analytics, which uses no cookies and doesn't identify you. Email alerts. If you sign up, we keep your email address and what you chose to follow, so we can send the emails. Every email has a link to change or stop them. To have your address deleted entirely, email us. Contact form. Your message, name and email come to us by email so we can answer. They aren't added to any list. API. Requests to the public API are logged with the caller's IP address for 90 days to stop abuse, then deleted. My Address. Address lookups go straight from your browser to Bay County's and FEMA's public map servers. BayCounty.me doesn't receive or store what you look up. The iPhone app No data collected. The app has no accounts, analytics or advertising, and sends nothing about you to BayCounty.me. Your address and location. If you save a home address, it stays on your phone. If you tap "Use my location," the app asks permission first and uses your location once to find your address on Bay County's public map server. It isn't stored or sent anywhere else. Downloaded data. The app saves copies of the public records it shows so it works offline. Deleting the app deletes them. Crash reports. If you've allowed it in your iPhone settings, Apple may share anonymous crash reports with the developer. Questions Email hello@fluxlabs.net or use the contact form . BayCounty.me is run by Flux Labs in Panama City, Florida.

x: Public Money · Map Public money on one map Redevelopment agency (CRA) spending and half-cent sales tax projects across Bay County, with the CRA district lines and city limits. Tap any mark to see the record and where it came from. The simple version What the marks mean Diamonds are CRA records: money a city's redevelopment agency spent, committed or budgeted inside its districts. Records with no address sit at the middle of their district. Dots are sales tax projects: roads, bridges, drainage and sidewalks paid for with the infrastructure half-cent, from the county's project map. Road projects sit at the middle of the road segment. Colors show status. Green is spent or finished, blue is under way, gray is planned. Hurricane Michael projects aren't on the map because the FEMA records don't give locations; they're on the Hurricane Michael page. The map Any status Spent / completed Committed / in progress Budgeted, proposed or not started CRA records (159) Sales tax projects (1,062) CRA districts City limits + − Show all CRA records come from the CRA Spending ledger, and district lines from Bay County GIS (including the 2025 St. Andrews expansion areas). Projects come from the county's sales tax project map on the Sales Tax Projects page; where a project matches a line in the county's program schedule, its programmed dollars are shown. City limits are from the U.S. Census Bureau.

The extra property tax a neighborhood brings in because its property became worth more after the CRA started. That extra is what fills the CRA's jar.
The starting snapshot of how much all the property in a CRA was worth. Only growth above this number pays into the CRA.
The CRA's own bank account. Tax increment goes in, and by law it can only be spent on that CRA's plan.
The day a CRA is scheduled to end. After that, the extra tax money goes back to the city and county budgets.
A deal where the CRA gives a builder back part of the new taxes their project creates, for a set number of years, to help get the project built.
Money a CRA gives a business owner to fix up the front of their building, usually matching what the owner spends.
A tax based on what your house or land is worth. More valuable property pays more.
Any government allowed to put a property tax on your bill, like the county, the school board or your city.
How property tax rates are written. One mill means $1 of tax for every $1,000 your property is taxed on.
The Property Appraiser's estimate of what your property would sell for.
Your property's value after any limits on how fast it can go up. For a homestead, it usually rises more slowly than the market.
The number your tax is actually figured on: the assessed value minus any exemptions.
A discount on property taxes for the home you live in full time, as long as you apply for it.
The tax rate that would bring in the same money as last year from the same properties. If a government picks a higher rate, the law calls it a tax increase, even if the rate didn't change.
The postcard you get each August showing your proposed taxes and when the public hearings are.
A flat fee on your tax bill for a service, like garbage pickup or fire protection. It isn't based on what your property is worth.
An extra county tax area that pays for services in only part of the county, usually the areas outside cities.
The school tax rate the state tells every school district to charge so it can get its share of state school money.
A limit on how fast a homestead's taxed value can go up: 3% a year, or less if inflation is lower. Rentals, businesses and second homes have a looser 10% limit.
The state's team of economists that estimates how much money a new law or amendment would add or take away.
The total property tax a government collects in a year: its rate times all the taxable value in its area.
A government's budget year. In Florida it runs from October 1 to September 30.
A government's main checking account for everyday services like police, parks and running city hall.
An account for a service you pay for directly, like water and sewer. The bills you pay cover the service.
Money that by law can only be spent on one thing, like gas tax for roads or a CRA's trust fund.
Money the state collects, mostly from sales tax, and sends back to cities and counties.
Money a government earns by charging for things it provides, like water bills, garbage pickup, permits and park fees.
Money one government gets from another, like federal grants or state shared revenue.
The elected county officials named in Florida's constitution: the sheriff, property appraiser, tax collector, clerk of court and supervisor of elections.
A yearly check of a government's books by outside accountants, to make sure the numbers add up and the rules were followed.
The record says the money was actually paid out.
A contract or award has been approved, but not all of the money has been paid yet.
Money set aside in a plan. It may or may not be spent.
An idea or request that hasn't been approved.
Shown on the site, but not added into the totals, so the same dollar is never counted twice.
An approved change to a contract after it is signed, which often adds cost or time.
The land a road sits on plus the strip alongside it for sidewalks, utilities and drainage.
When a government buys private land for a public project even if the owner doesn't want to sell. A court decides the fair price.
A way for a government to borrow money now and pay it back with interest over many years, like a mortgage.
A special government created for one development to build and pay for its roads, pipes and other basics. The property owners there pay for it.
A contract between two governments, like a city and the county.
Asking a government to show you or send you its records. In Florida, anyone can ask, and you don't have to say why.
A government's list of every payment it made: who got paid, how much, when and for what.

t: Bay County: Lack of Documented Review of Required Quarterly Reports (federal, AL 97.036 FEMA Public Assistance)
s: 3 of 40 quarterly FEMA (Hurricane Michael) reports prepared by the county's consultant did not match approved expenses and support. There was no documented county review before the consultant submitted them. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Bay County: Ineligible Expenses Approved for Reimbursement (federal, AL 97.083 SAFER fire staffing grant)
s: Two of three reimbursement requests tested included ineligible payroll costs approved by the grant administrator. The federal grantor caught them and paid only eligible costs. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Bay County: Material audit adjustments (Bay County financial statements)
s: Material adjustments were needed for the financial statements to meet GAAP because county controls did not catch them in time. Material weakness.

t: Bay County: Material adjustments - Bay County Property Appraiser
s: The Property Appraiser's office needed material adjustments to cash and accounts payable, and a check was improperly dated in its records. Material weakness.

t: Bay County: Permit fees not charged per adopted fee schedule (first reported 2020)
s: Because of problems in the permit system, the county charged some permit fees that did not match the fee schedule set by Resolutions 3945 and 3957, overcharging in some cases; the county booked a payable for the estimated excess. Auditor recommended fixing the system and remedying affected permits.

t: Bay County: Material adjustments - Bay County Sheriff
s: The Sheriff's office needed material adjustments to cash, expenses, unearned revenue, payables and accrued liabilities. Material weakness.

t: Bay County: Permit fees not charged per adopted fee schedule (Resolution 3847)
s: Permit system errors caused some permits to be charged above the adopted fee schedule.

t: Bay County: Inadequate review of component unit financial information
s: The county did not adequately review figures from a discretely presented component unit, so adjustments were needed. Significant deficiency.

t: Bay County: Material adjustments - Bay County Sheriff (repeat of 2021-001)
s: Sheriff's office needed material audit adjustments.

t: Bay District Schools: Audit Adjusting Entries (first reported 2024)
s: Significant corrections were needed, including unearned state funds not identified, an unrecorded IT subscription agreement, misclassified capital spending, and OPEB, accrual and lease adjustments. The auditor ties it partly to a lack of appropriate staffing.

t: Bay District Schools: Expenditures not limited to budgeted amounts (first reported by Auditor General as AM 2023-001)
s: General Fund spending exceeded the budget in three functional categories by a total of $326,700, and the Board did not amend the budget by September 10 as state law and Board policy require. Caused by year-end adjustments not reflected in budget monitoring.

t: Bay District Schools: Return of Title IV funds worksheets not documented as independently reviewed (federal, Pell Grant, Haney Technical College)
s: Refunds of federal student aid were calculated correctly, but there was no sign-off showing an independent review. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Bay District Schools: Return of Title IV funds not made within required timeline (federal, Pell Grant)
s: For 2 of 9 students tested, federal aid was returned to the U.S. Department of Education after the 45-day deadline because of manual-control human error. Could risk future Pell funding. Significant deficiency.

t: Bay District Schools: Multi-factor authentication not required for student information (federal, Pell / Gramm-Leach-Bliley)
s: The district's system did not require multi-factor authentication to access student information, as federal student-information security rules require. Material weakness.

t: Bay District Schools: Lack of Appropriate Staffing Leading to Audit Entries
s: Staffing shortfalls meant the district's own processes missed entries the auditors had to make. Material weakness.

t: Bay District Schools: Wage rate (Davis-Bacon) compliance (federal, COVID-19 Education Stabilization Fund AL 84.425)
s: Two construction contracts shifted mid-stream to federal pandemic funds lacked the required Davis-Bacon wage clause, and certified payrolls were not collected. Questioned costs: $773,629. Significant deficiency.

t: Bay District Schools: Expenditures not limited to budgeted amounts (repeat of AM 2023-001)
s: General Fund spending again exceeded budgeted function amounts without a timely Board amendment.
General Fund spending exceeded budgeted amounts in six functional categories by $9,532 to $218,198 (total $582,437) and the Board did not amend the budget by September 10.

t: Panama City: CRA policies, procedures and plan documents (previously 2022-002, 2023-001)
s: The city's Community Redevelopment Agency's policies, procedures and plan documents did not ensure expenditures were proper; assets could be misused or unallowable spending could occur. Reported as a material weakness.

t: Panama City: CRA policies, procedures and plan documents (previously 2022-002)
s: Same CRA policy deficiency as above.
Asset tags were missing on several capital assets and some assets could not be found for testing; procedures did not ensure assets were tagged or properly disposed of.
Bank accounts were not reconciled on a timely, regular basis, risking misappropriation or misstated records.

t: Panama City: CRA policies, procedures and plan documents
s: CRA policies did not ensure expenditures were proper.

t: Panama City: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards and State Financial Assistance (previously 2021-008)
s: Inadequate procedures to prepare the federal/state grant spending schedule, so misstatements might not be caught.
Inadequate capital asset policies (tagging, disposals).

t: Panama City: Late federal data collection form (previously 2021-011)
s: The Single Audit data collection form was not submitted on time; agencies could withhold, suspend or terminate awards.
Related timeliness finding on required report submission (same corrective action as 2022-005).

t: Panama City Beach: Lack of Documented Review of Annual Project and Expenditure Report (federal, AL 21.027 COVID-19 State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds)
s: The annual ARPA project and expenditure report to the U.S. Treasury was prepared by the grant administrator with no documented second-person review. Material weakness in internal control over compliance; no questioned costs.

t: Panama City Beach: Lack of Documented Review of Quarterly Reports (state, CSFA 43.009 Local Government Fire Services Grants)
s: None of the quarterly state fire-grant reports tested showed a documented review before submission. Material weakness; no questioned costs.

t: Lynn Haven: Reconciliation of Account Balances, Audit Adjustments
s: Auditors had to correct journal entries to finish year-end balances, especially grant revenues and receivables, which also changed the federal/state awards schedule. Auditor cites turnover of key staff and late Hurricane Michael grant reimbursements, but noted significant improvement over the prior year.

t: Lynn Haven: Reconciliation of Account Balances and Audit Adjustments
s: Same issue; classified as a material weakness in FY2024.

t: Lynn Haven: Reconciliation of Account Balances and Audit Adjustments
s: Same issue; repeat of 2022-001; corrective action not taken.
The auditors had to make significant corrections to the city's books.

t: Springfield: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation (first reported 2007)
s: The city cannot prepare its own federal grant spending schedule; the auditors help, and multiple year-end grant entries were needed.
The pooled cash account in the ledger did not match the monthly and year-end bank reconciliations. Errors or fraud could go undetected.

t: Springfield: Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers (first reported 2015)
s: Receivables, customer deposits and payables did not agree with their detail ledgers and were not reconciled during the year.
The month-end checklist leaves out major balances, so monthly financial reports given to the Commission are not reliable.
Many revenues and expenses were posted to the wrong accounts or netted together, hiding what was really collected and spent.
Small staff means one person can approve, record and have custody of assets, including broad accounting system access.

t: Springfield: Actual Expenditures Exceeded Budget in the General Fund
s: General Fund spending exceeded the final adopted budget by about $8,069,872 without a budget amendment, violating s. 166.241(3) F.S. The auditor suggested budgeting for debt proceeds and similar sources (the year included the $15 million city complex loan).
Significant auditor corrections required.

t: Springfield: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation
s: City cannot prepare its federal awards schedule.
Cash in the ledger did not match bank reconciliations.

t: Springfield: Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers
s: Receivables, deposits and payables not reconciled to detail ledgers.
Incomplete month-end close.
Revenues and expenses misclassified or netted.
Incompatible duties not separated.

t: Springfield: Collection and Write-off Policies and Procedures (first reported 2020)
s: No written policy for sending unpaid accounts to collections or writing them off, so receivables may be overstated and customers treated inconsistently.

t: Springfield: Final Budget Not Approved Within the Allowed Time Period
s: The FY2024 budget was amended in February 2025, after the deadline in state law.

t: Springfield: Timely Reporting Requirements for Grants
s: Single Audit package not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse because of staffing shortages and the many corrections needed.

t: Springfield: Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund - City Allocation
s: Over three years the city did not calculate and pay its share of tax increment to its own CRA, underfunding the CRA trust fund by an estimated $291,027 (material weakness).
Significant auditor corrections required.

t: Springfield: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation
s: City cannot prepare its federal awards schedule.
Cash not reconciled to bank.

t: Springfield: Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers
s: Detail ledgers not reconciled.
Incomplete month-end close.
Incompatible duties not separated.

t: Springfield: Collection and Write-off Policies and Procedures
s: No written collections/write-off policy.
The auditors had to propose adjustments before the city's books met accounting standards (GAAP). Material weakness. First reported in 2007.

t: Parker: Lack of Segregation of Duties (first reported 2009)
s: Too few staff to separate incompatible duties; material weakness reported since 2009.

t: Parker: Reporting Requirements for Grants (first reported 2023)
s: The audit was not finished within 9 months of year end, so the federal Single Audit package was not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. The city could lose grant funding.

t: Parker: Insufficient Documentation Supporting Law Enforcement Trust Fund Revenue
s: The city booked $36,652 from disposed criminal-case evidence as Law Enforcement Trust Fund revenue but could not show a forfeiture judgment or court order proving the money legally belonged to the city. Revenue and fund balance may be overstated by $36,652.

t: Parker: Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund (first reported 2024)
s: State law (s. 163.387 F.S.) requires each taxing authority to pay its tax increment to the CRA by January 1. The county paid 4 days late and the city did not pay its own share before year end, leaving the CRA trust fund short about $122,929.
Employee data sent to the actuary for the retiree-health (OPEB) valuation had multiple errors, producing an inaccurate valuation and delaying the audit.

t: Parker: Retirement Expense Not Reviewed Timely and Rates Not Updated
s: The city did not update new state FRS contribution rates effective July 1, 2025 in its payroll system for months, understating retirement expense and liability by about $20,000.
Auditor-proposed adjustments needed to meet GAAP.

t: Parker: Lack of Segregation of Duties
s: Too few staff to separate duties.

t: Parker: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards
s: Weak controls over preparing the financial statements and the federal awards schedule (material weakness); repeat of 2023-003 and 2022-003.

t: Parker: Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund - City Allocation
s: For the current year and the two years before, the city did not calculate and transfer its required share of tax increment to its CRA.
Single Audit package not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse.
Inaccurate employee data given to the OPEB actuary.

t: Parker: Lack of Review and Reconciliation of Certain Account Activity
s: Certain account activity was not consistently reviewed and reconciled.

t: Parker: Reimbursement Requests Not Formally Approved Before Submission (federal, AL 97.036 FEMA Public Assistance)
s: Hurricane Michael FEMA reimbursement requests were submitted without documented city approval. Significant deficiency in internal control over compliance; no questioned costs.
Auditor-proposed adjustments needed to meet GAAP.

t: Parker: Lack of Segregation of Duties
s: Too few staff to separate duties.

t: Parker: Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards
s: Weak controls over preparing the financial statements and federal awards schedule (material weakness).
Incomplete payroll information was sent to the state with the June 2023 Florida Retirement System report, risking wrong contributions and pension balances.

t: Parker: Incomplete List of Capital Asset Deletions
s: The city first gave the auditor an incomplete list of assets sold or disposed of, which risks inaccurate asset records and misuse of equipment.
Single Audit package not filed on time.

t: Mexico Beach: Management Override and Segregation of Duties (sixth-year repeat)
s: The finance office is too small, and had turnover, so the same person could prepare and approve adjusting journal entries. Errors or misstatements could go undetected.
No budget was legally adopted for the Disaster Recovery Fund, even though state law requires spending to follow an adopted budget.
Impact fees were not kept in a separate fund, as s. 163.31801 F.S. requires.
Building department spending is not budgeted or tracked separately, so the city cannot show it complies with the state cap on carrying forward building permit fees (s. 553.80(7)(a) F.S.).
The bond sinking fund was underfunded at year end, which breaks the bond covenants.

t: Mexico Beach: Deficit in Unrestricted Net Position
s: The utility (enterprise) funds ended the year with a deficit in unrestricted net position, meaning liabilities exceed the assets available for general use. The auditor suggests rate changes, cost control or better long-term planning.

t: Mexico Beach: Compliance with State Reporting Requirements
s: The city missed the Nov. 30 deadline for the annual Public Depositor Report to the state CFO (risking state protection of public deposits), and an elected official filed the annual financial disclosure with the Commission on Ethics late.

t: Mexico Beach: Management Override and Segregation of Duties (fifth-year repeat)
s: Same segregation-of-duties weakness as above; reported as a significant deficiency.

t: Mexico Beach: Reconciliation of Account Balances and Audit Adjustments (fifth-year repeat)
s: Account balances were not fully reconciled and the auditor had to propose adjustments; reported as a significant deficiency.
The city had no policy to collect and hold customer utility deposits.
Not all funds had legally adopted budgets.
Impact fees not in a separate fund.
Building department costs not budgeted/tracked separately.
Bond covenant requirements (sinking fund) not met.

t: Mexico Beach: Deficit in Unrestricted Net Position
s: Enterprise funds reported a deficit in unrestricted net position.

t: Mexico Beach: Management Override and Segregation of Duties (fourth-year repeat)
s: Segregation-of-duties weakness; reported as a material weakness.

t: Mexico Beach: Reconciliation of Account Balances and Audit Adjustments (fourth-year repeat)
s: Balances not reconciled; auditor adjustments needed; material weakness.

t: Mexico Beach: Timeliness of Bank Reconciliations (fourth-year repeat)
s: Bank reconciliations were not prepared promptly; material weakness.
Not all funds had legally adopted budgets.
No policy to collect and hold customer utility deposits.

t: Mexico Beach: Building Permit Expenditures (fourth-year repeat)
s: Building department costs not tracked against the state carry-forward cap.
Bond covenant requirements not met.

t: Mexico Beach: Impact Fee Accounting (second-year repeat)
s: Impact fees not in a separate fund.

t: Panama City CRA: Review of Policies and Procedures (previously 2022-002, 2023-001)
s: The CRA's policies, procedures and plan documents had several deficiencies, and it did not keep proper documentation showing it complied with Florida Statutes. Auditor recommends updating policies and plans and verifying compliance with statutes and grant rules. Material weakness.

t: Panama City CRA: Review of Policies and Procedures (previously 2022-002)
s: Same policy and statutory-documentation deficiencies; material weakness.
The high-volume concentration bank account was not reconciled on time during the year. Material weakness.

t: Panama City CRA: Review of Policies and Procedures
s: Policy, plan and statutory-compliance documentation deficiencies. Material weakness.
